case1_no_timeout.conclusion: The fault is scheduled, Toxiproxy visibly has a dep_slow_latency toxic active on a 'dep:9090' proxy during the run (confirmed live via the Toxiproxy control API), and the run completes with correctly-evaluated thresholds -- but the SUT's actual traffic never passes through that proxy at all, so the injected 3s latency has zero effect on measured request timing (max observed: 10.67ms, even with the fault window widened to 35s against a 45s load phase to remove any timing-overlap doubt). This is not a timing artifact; it is defect C below.

defect_C.title: egress.Classify silently drops a user-declared egress.hosts entry for any host detect.Detect's closed image vocabulary does not recognize -- the R-EXE-20 fault-interception rename then never fires, and the fault never reaches its target
defect_C.severity: critical for E1 specifically: it means a fault targeting any custom, non-database/cache/broker internal dependency (i.e. any ordinary service-to-service HTTP call between two of the user's own services -- exactly case 1's shape, 'HTTP client with no timeout') can never actually be delivered, on any torture.yaml, regardless of how the fixture is built.
defect_C.root_cause: internal/egress/egress.go's Classify(detected, cfg) iterates `for host, dclass := range detected` -- detected is detect.System.EgressClass, populated only for compose services whose image matches detect's closed R-DET-9 vocabulary (postgres*, redis*, kafka*, ...; see internal/detect/compose.go's imagePatterns). A host the user explicitly classifies in torture.yaml's egress.hosts (cfg.Hosts) but that detect never put in `detected` is never visited by this loop, so it is silently absent from the returned classes map entirely -- not 'internal', not 'unclassified', just missing. internal/run.internalNetworkFaultTargets then filters it out (classes[target] != ClassInternal), so ComposeTopologyApplier.Apply's R-EXE-20 rename-and-alias never happens for that host: the original service keeps running under its real name, and the SUT's traffic reaches it directly, bypassing the Toxiproxy proxy the fault was applied to.
empirical_confirmation: docker compose config on the applied overlay shows the 'dep' service with no `profiles:` key and no 'dep-tortureu-backend' clone service at all -- the R-EXE-20 rename never happened.
docker ps confirms the ORIGINAL 'dep' container (case*-dep-1) is running, aliased 'dep', at a different IP than the proxy.
docker exec into checkout-api's container shows /etc/hosts resolves 'dep' directly to the original dep container's IP (172.22.0.2), not the proxy's IP (172.22.0.3).

Toxiproxy's own control API shows the dep_slow_latency toxic genuinely applied and active on a 'dep:9090' proxy -- the fault *was* scheduled and applied by internal/run's own separate ensureProxy-on-first-toxic path -- but nothing ever dials that proxy, so the toxic has no observable effect.
Same result twice: once with the corpus's designed 20s/15s timing, once with the window widened to 45s/35s specifically to rule out a timing-overlap explanation.
defect_C.owner: internal/egress (Classify) and/or internal/detect (the closed image vocabulary Classify's outer loop is keyed to) -- both out of this task's edit scope. Reported, not patched.
defect_C.scope_beyond_case_1: Any corpus case whose target is a custom application service (not postgres/mysql/redis/mongo/kafka/rabbitmq/etc.) will hit this identically. Cases 3 (postgres pool) and 7 (redis cache stampede) target recognized image types and should be unaffected; case 4 (queue consumer) likely targets a recognized broker image and should also be unaffected. Cases 2 and 5, depending on how they're built, may or may not hit this -- not yet built.
